```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(simdfuse)
```

## The problem

R evaluates an array expression one operator at a time. Each operator reads its
inputs from memory, allocates a fresh vector, writes the result, and hands it to
the next operator. For

```r
a * b + sqrt(c) - 2.5
```

that is three temporary vectors of length `n` and four traversals of memory. The
arithmetic itself is nearly free; what costs is moving data. Once the vectors are
larger than the last-level cache, the expression runs at the speed of the memory
bus, and the only way to go faster is to traverse less.

`simdfuse` compiles the expression into a short instruction stream and evaluates
it one cache-resident block at a time, so every intermediate value lives and dies
in L1 cache:

```{r}
a <- runif(1e5); b <- runif(1e5); c <- runif(1e5)

identical(sf(a * b + sqrt(c) - 2.5), a * b + sqrt(c) - 2.5)
```

Note `identical`, not `all.equal`. By default the result is bit-for-bit what base
R produces; see `vignette("accuracy")` for exactly what that promise covers.

## What you can write

Anything built from the functions in `sf_supported()`, plus numeric literals and
double, integer or logical vectors. Unsupported calls are a compile-time error
with a message naming the offending function, never a silent fallback:

```{r, error = TRUE}
sf(quantile(a, 0.5) + 1)
```

## Reductions that allocate nothing

The reduction forms never build a result vector at all. `sum((x - mu)^2)` in base
R materialises two full-length temporaries; the fused form holds a few kilobytes
whatever the length of `x`:

```

Integer and logical vectors are read in their own storage rather than coerced
first. The block loader converts each block as it copies into a register --
work it was doing anyway -- so there is no second vector the size of the input
and no extra pass over it. `NA_integer_` becomes `NA_real_`, so `is.na()` and
base R agree.

The side effect is that an integer input is *cheaper* than the equivalent
double, because there is half as much of it to read:

```{r}
iv <- sample(1:1000L, 2e6, TRUE)
dv <- as.double(iv)
rbind(integer = system.time(for (i in 1:20) sf_sum(quote(iv * 2)))[["elapsed"]],
      double  = system.time(for (i in 1:20) sf_sum(quote(dv * 2)))[["elapsed"]])
```

```{r}
x <- rnorm(1e5); mu <- mean(x)
sf_sum(~ (x - mu)^2)
```

A Gaussian log-likelihood is the idiomatic case. Written out, it is five
operations and a sum; fused, it is one pass and no allocation:

```{r}
s <- sd(x)
sf_sum(~ -0.5 * log(2 * pi) - log(s) - 0.5 * ((x - mu) / s)^2)
```

The scalars here (`pi`, `s`, `mu`) are hoisted out of the loop automatically, so
the two logarithms are evaluated once per call rather than once per element.
`sf_compile()` shows what the engine actually does:

```{r}
sf_compile(~ -0.5 * log(2 * pi) - log(s) - 0.5 * ((x - mu) / s)^2,
           scalars = c("pi", "s", "mu"))
```

For an expression evaluated many times -- inside an optimiser, a bootstrap, an
MCMC step -- compile it once:

```{r}
nll <- sf_kernel(~ 0.5 * ((x - mu) / s)^2 + log(s), reduce = "sum")
nll(x = x, mu = 0, s = 1)
```

## Skeletons

Three parallel constructs that base R does not provide, each consuming an
expression rather than a stored vector.

A prefix scan under any associative operator, including a numerically stable
log-domain one:

```{r}
lp <- c(800, 801, 802)       # exp(800) overflows a double
sf_scan(~ lp, "logsumexp")
log(cumsum(exp(lp)))         # the naive form gives up
```

A weighted stencil. `weights[1]` multiplies the earliest element of the window,
so `c(-1/2, 0, 1/2)` reads as a centred first difference:

```{r}
y <- cumsum(rnorm(50))
head(sf_stencil(~ y, c(-1/2, 0, 1/2), boundary = "replicate"), 4)
```

A reduction within contiguous runs, which is the shape of a sorted panel:

```{r}
value <- c(1, 2, 3, 10, 20, 100)
firm  <- c(1, 1, 1,  2,  2,   3)
sf_segreduce(~ value^2, firm, "sum")
```

Segments are *runs*, not groups: sort by the identifier first if the data are not
already grouped. That restriction is what keeps the operation single-pass.

## Checking what you are running on

```{r}
sf_info()
```

The engine builds one kernel per instruction set and picks among them at load
time from the CPU's reported features. You can pin a narrower one, which is
useful for reproducing results across machines with different hardware:

```{r}
old <- sf_options(isa = "sse2")$isa
sf_info()$isa
sf_options(isa = old)
```
